query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles, maintaining structural and chemical stability across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges (473–1923 K) is governed by a balance between the configurational entropy that stabilizes the uniformly mixed bulk and the tendency of elements with lower cohesive/d‐band energies (e.g., Cu and Pd) to segregate to the surface to minimize internal energy.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals (e.g., Pd, Cu, Pt, Ni, Co) in near‐equal atomic ratios with a homogeneous elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Thermal annealing of the nanoparticles at controlled temperatures and dwell times across the 473–1923 K range to activate atomic diffusion and induce surface segregation.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under inert atmosphere (to avoid oxidation) and without additional chemical modifiers, ensuring that observed changes are due solely to temperature-driven atomic dynamics.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree and pattern of surface segregation, specifically the enrichment of metals with lower cohesive energies (e.g., Cu and Pd) at the surface versus retention of high cohesive energy elements (e.g., Co, Ni, Pt) in the bulk.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, increased atomic mobility allows certain elements (with lower intrinsic cohesive contributions via d‐band effects) to preferentially migrate to the nanoparticle surface, reducing overall internal energy. Simultaneously, the high configurational entropy of the mixed bulk resists phase separation. The resulting moderate surface segregation is hypothesized to optimize interfacial energetics and preserve the overall solid-solution stability, thereby maintaining catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles that exhibit controlled, moderate surface segregation (with Cu and Pd enriched at the surface, but with a uniformly mixed bulk) will retain stable catalytic and thermoelectric properties over the temperature range, whereas samples with either no segregation or excessive segregation (leading to phase separation) will display diminished performance.
generation.baseline: As-synthesized solid-solution nanoparticles with uniform elemental distribution before thermal treatment.
generation.boundary: If the thermal treatment is excessively prolonged or at too high temperatures such that extreme atomic diffusion leads to complete phase separation (loss of the solid-solution structure) or, conversely, if the temperature/duration is insufficient to induce any segregation, then the predicted performance enhancement will not be observed.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between the degree of surface segregation and the optimal performance window is not clearly defined, and the critical annealing temperatures/dwell times that balance these effects remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HEA nanoparticle samples and subject them to a range of thermal annealing protocols (varying temperature and dwell time) within 473–1923 K. Characterize the elemental distributions across the surface and bulk using techniques such as XPS and atom-probe tomography. Simultaneously, measure catalytic activity (e.g., ORR performance) and thermoelectric properties. Compare samples with moderate surface segregation against those with either minimal or excessive segregation.
measurements: Surface and bulk elemental composition profiles
Catalytic performance metrics (e.g., reaction rates, onset potentials)
Thermoelectric efficiency parameters (e.g., Seebeck coefficient, electrical conductivity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles that do not exhibit the predicted moderate surface segregation (or remain entirely uniform) match or exceed the stability and performance of those with controlled segregation, then the hypothesis that the balance between bulk configurational entropy and surface segregation governs stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To assess the surface stability of our HEA system under annealing conditions, we employed machine learning interatomic potentials based on graph neural networks, particularly the atomistic line graph neural network (ALIGNN), in molecular simulations to obtain equilibrium configurations. Details of model development can be found in the Method section. Figure 3a presents a parity plot comparing DFT-calculated and ALIGNN-predicted per-atom energies. Both training and test data sets exhibit mean absolute errors (MAEs) below 5 meV/atom, indicating a balanced model without noticeable underfitting or overfitting. To determine the equilibrium surface configurations after high-temperature annealing, canonical Monte Carlo simulations were conducted using the trained deep learning potential, with an equilibrium achieved after approximately 16,000 steps. The underlying mechanisms driving Cu and Pd segregation can be elucidated through Helmholtz free energy components F = U – TS of canonical ensembles, encompassing internal energy (U) and entropy (S). According to the cohesion theory, the cohesive energy trend among late transition and noble metals is mainly dictated by the d-band, approximated as where Wd represents the d-band width and Nd is the number of d-electrons. For Cu, with a fully occupied d-band (Nd = 10), its cohesive contribution is minimal, making metallic bonds with Cu energetically less favorable. Consequently, to minimize the system’s internal energy, Cu atoms tend to segregate onto the surface. Pd has only marginally higher cohesive and surface energies compared to Cu, which partially contributes to the surface segregation of Pd. Moreover, given the abundance of Pd in the HEA’s bulk composition (Pd0.25Cu0.20Pt0.20Ni0.22Co0.13 as targeted in our simulations), segregation to the surface occurs as the bulk strives for an equimolar distribution to maximize the configurational entropy, thereby rationalizing the segregation of Pd atoms at the HEA surface as observed in Monte Carlo simulations.
